Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one.

Read the passage and answer the questions: "The truth of the self-conscious individual lies not in its immediate certainty, but in the dialectical movement of its becoming. Consciousness, in its pursuit of knowledge, initially assumes that its object is something external and independent. Yet, through the labor of experience, it discovers that this object is not truly separate but is mediated by consciousness itself. The apparent duality of subject and object is thus sublated in the dialectic, revealing that knowledge is not the passive reception of an external truth but an active process in which consciousness shapes and transforms its own reality. This movement unfolds through a series of contradictions, in which each stage of consciousness, believing itself to have attained certainty, encounters its own inadequacy. The master-slave dialectic exemplifies this: self-consciousness seeks recognition from another, yet in asserting its dominance over the other, it paradoxically undermines its own freedom. The master, in reducing the slave to a mere instrument, deprives himself of a fully realized recognition. Meanwhile, the slave, through labor and self-transformation, attains a deeper awareness of autonomy, demonstrating that freedom is not given but achieved through negation and overcoming.

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "The explanation of a work is always sought in the man or woman who produced it, as if it were always, in the end, through the voice of a single person that literature spoke: through the voice of a single person and the imprints of his or her passions. The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author, his life, his history, and his intentions. But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. This radical displacement shifts the power from the creator to the interpreter, from the supposed intention of the writer to the infinite play of signifiers within the text itself.

question.en:
"The idea that space and time form a four-dimensional continuum was first suggested by Hermann Minkowski as a natural consequence of Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity. In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity."

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: The argument of this book is that we, and all other animals, are machines created by our genes. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived sometimes for millions of years in a highly competitive world. This has entailed ruthless selfishness in gene selection, yet paradoxically it has also favored behaviors that, at an organismal level, may appear cooperative or even altruistic. The key to understanding this paradox lies in recognizing that what matters is not the survival of the individual organism, nor even the species, but rather the continuity of the genes themselves. Natural selection, therefore, operates at the level of replicators-genes-rather than the individual creatures they construct as temporary vehicles. These survival machines, whether they be humans, ants, or oak trees, serve merely as the means through which genes propagate. This gene-centered view of evolution helps explain many otherwise puzzling phenomena in nature. For example, kin selection provides a compelling reason why apparent acts of altruism, such as worker ants sacrificing their ability to reproduce, can evolve: by ensuring the survival and reproduction of closely related individuals, an organism still promotes the continuity of its genetic lineage. This perspective challenges the common anthropocentric tendency to view evolution as a process geared toward the 'good of the species. In reality, natural selection cares nothing for abstract collective welfare; it blindly favors gene variants that are better at replicating, regardless of their consequences beyond that singular goal.

1.en: The tapestry featured gules and argent prominently.

2.en: The chef prepared a sauce of deep gules and cumin.

3.en: The gules border signified martial lineage.

4.en: The herald explained the symbolism of gules to visitors.

solution.en:
The highlighted word **gules** refers to the heraldic color red. In the original sentence, it is used in the context of a coat of arms. A homonym is a word with the same spelling and pronunciation but different meanings.
**The chef prepared a sauce of deep gules and cumin.** Here, **gules** is a homonym as it is used to describe a deep red color or ingredient in a sauce, rather than the heraldic symbol. The other options use it in the same heraldic sense.
Correct Answer is **The chef prepared a sauce of deep gules and cumin.** because it uses the homonym of the highlighted word.
**Ans: The chef prepared a sauce of deep gules and cumin.**

Read the passage and answer the questions: It is with the gravest import that we relay intelligence from the Continent, where the machinations of foreign Powers betoken a perturbation most grievous to the tranquillity of Europe. Reports reaching our office, albeit through channels of dubious veracity, intimate that certain Ministers of State, long disaffected, have entered into clandestine parley, thereby imperilling the precarious Peace recently brokered at Amiens. The populace, though desirous of repose after protracted tumult, remains uneasy; their apprehensions stoked by pamphleteers whose incendiary declamations find ready purchase amongst the credulous. Meanwhile, at Westminster, the Commons are engaged in fervid debate upon the propriety of augmenting naval armaments, lest perfidious designs render our shores vulnerable. It is the sentiment of many learned gentlemen that vigilance, tempered with prudence, is the surest safeguard against the perfidy of hostile ambition. Further dispatches are awaited with no small degree of trepidation."

Which term refers to "The psychological phenomenon in which people are more likely to commit unethical acts when they feel their actions are not being observed"?

solution.en:
**Deindividuation (अव्यक्तिकरण)** = a psychological phenomenon in which people are more likely to commit unethical acts when they feel their actions are not being observed.

**Moral Disengagement (नैतिक अलगाव)** = deactivating moral self-regulation → It is not the required meaning.
Correct Answer is **Deindividuation** because it refers to the loss of self-awareness in anonymous situations, leading to unethical behaviour.
**Ans: Deindividuation**

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one.

question.en:
In today's fast-paced world, staying fit and healthy has become more important than ever. Regular exercise helps improve physical strength, mental well-being, and overall energy levels. A combination of cardio exercises, such as running or cycling, and strength training can help keep the body in good shape. Apart from exercise, maintaining a balanced diet plays a crucial role in fitness. Eating fresh fruits, vegetables, and protein-rich foods provides essential nutrients for the body. On the other hand, consuming excessive junk food can lead to health problems like obesity and heart disease. Fitness is not just about physical health; it also impacts mental well-being. Regular workouts release endorphins, which help reduce stress and improve mood. Even simple activities like walking or stretching can make a big difference. Staying fit requires dedication and consistency, but the benefits are worth the effort.

Identify the sentence with correct subject-verb agreement:

[Selection Post Phase XIII (10th), 29 Aug 2025, Shift 3]

1.en: Regular exercises helps in maintaining fitness.

2.en: The benefits of daily workouts is numerous.

3.en: A balanced diet and exercise are important for health.

4.en: Eating junk food lead to health issues.

solution.en:
**Rule:** Subject-verb agreement requires the verb to match the subject in number. In option (c), "A balanced diet and exercise" is a compound subject, which is plural, so the plural verb "are" is correct.
Correct Answer is **A balanced diet and exercise are important for health.** because the subject is plural and agrees with the verb.
**Ans: A balanced diet and exercise are important for health.**

question.en: <div>Which of the following sentences correctly uses the idiom &quot;a slip of the tongue&quot;?&nbsp;</div> [Steno, 06 Aug 2026, Shift 1]

1.en: The chef burned his hand and let out a slip of the tongue.

2.en: Sneha carefully planned her speech to ensure a slip of the tongue.

3.en: Sunita lost her balance while walking and had a slip of the tongue.

4.en: Ravi misspoke during the interview; it was just a slip of the tongue.

solution.en:
**A slip of the tongue (जुबान फिसलना)** = an unintentional mistake made in speaking.
**The chef burned his hand and let out a slip of the tongue.** → Incorrect usage (pain is not a slip of the tongue).
**Sneha carefully planned her speech to ensure a slip of the tongue.** → Incorrect (you don't plan a mistake).
**Sunita lost her balance while walking and had a slip of the tongue.** → Incorrect (not a verbal error).
**Ravi misspoke during the interview; it was just a slip of the tongue.** = he made a verbal error → It is the correct usage.
Correct Answer is **Ravi misspoke during the interview; it was just a slip of the tongue.** because it correctly describes a verbal mistake.
**Ans: Ravi misspoke during the interview; it was just a slip of the tongue.**

question.en: <div><!-- x-tinymce/html -->Which of the following sentences correctly uses the idiom <strong>&quot;A picture is worth a thousand words&quot;?</strong></div> [Steno, 07 Aug 2026, Shift 1]

1.en: I prefer reading detailed descriptions rather than looking at images, even though a picture is worth a thousand words.

2.en: The beautiful photograph captured the tragedy so well that no words were needed-truly, a picture is worth a thousand words.

3.en: Since she couldn&#39;t take a picture, she decided to write a long paragraph, as a picture is worth a thousand words.

4.en: He described the entire scene in detail because a picture is worth a thousand words.

solution.en:
**A picture is worth a thousand words (एक तस्वीर हज़ार शब्दों के बराबर होती है)** = a single image can convey a complex idea or emotion better than words.
**I prefer reading detailed descriptions rather than looking at images, even though a picture is worth a thousand words.** → Contradicts the idiom.
**The beautiful photograph captured the tragedy so well that no words were needed-truly, a picture is worth a thousand words.** = the image explains everything → It is the correct usage.
**Since she couldn't take a picture, she decided to write a long paragraph, as a picture is worth a thousand words.** → Incorrect usage.
**He described the entire scene in detail because a picture is worth a thousand words.** → Contradicts the idiom.
Correct Answer is **The beautiful photograph captured the tragedy so well that no words were needed-truly, a picture is worth a thousand words.** because it shows the power of the image.
**Ans: The beautiful photograph captured the tragedy so well that no words were needed-truly, a picture is worth a thousand words.**

question.en:
<strong>Select the correct option:</strong><br />
The journalist refused to ___ her sources despite repeated legal threats. [CGL, 14 Sep 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en: <strong>Correct Answer: Give out</strong><br /><br />**Give out (जानकारी देना/प्रकट करना)** = to reveal, disclose, or make information known, especially information that is confidential or not generally known.<br /><br /><strong>Important Points:</strong><br />• **Give out** = to reveal, disclose, or make something known; it can also mean distribute or stop functioning depending on the context.<br />• **Give away** = to reveal a secret or information, or to give something to someone for free. Although 'give away' can have a similar meaning, it is not the intended answer in this SSC question.<br />• **Give over** = to hand or transfer something to someone; it can also mean to stop doing something.<br />• **Give up** = to quit, surrender, or stop trying.<br /><br /><strong>Detailed Explanation:</strong><br />The journalist's sources are confidential people who provide information. The sentence means that the journalist refused to **give out** or **disclose** the identity/information about her sources despite repeated legal threats. Therefore, **give out** is the correct option according to the intended SSC answer.<br /><br /><strong>Additional Information:</strong><br />**Give out** has several meanings depending on context:<br />• To distribute: *The teacher gave out the question papers.*<br />• To reveal/disclose information: *He refused to give out confidential information.*<br />• To stop functioning: *The engine suddenly gave out.*<br /><br />In this question, the meaning is **to disclose/reveal information**, so **give out** is correct.<br /><br /><strong>Ans: Give out</strong>

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is based on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Scientists take great pains to defend that assumption, often restricting their vision to the phenomena that the existing paradigm has defined as relevant. When research proceeds in this fashion, findings tend to be incremental, reinforcing the established framework rather than challenging it. Yet, over time, anomalies-empirical observations that cannot be explained within the current paradigm-accumulate. Initially, these anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure. However, as these anomalies grow in number and significance, they begin to erode confidence in the prevailing paradigm. The resolution of such crises is not a straightforward process of falsification, as Popper might suggest, but rather a transformation in the very way scientists see the world. Scientific revolutions occur when a new paradigm emerges-one that is not merely an extension of the old but a fundamental reconceptualization of reality. This shift is not purely logical or empirical; it involves a radical change in perspective, akin to a gestalt switch. The Copernican Revolution, for example, did not merely adjust astronomical calculations; it redefined the very framework through which celestial motion was understood. Similarly, Einstein's theory of relativity did not just modify Newtonian mechanics but replaced its foundational assumptions about space and time.

question.en:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.
He will ___ the award at the ceremony tomorrow. [DP HCM]

solution.en:
Correct option (b)

The correct answer is 'accept'.
 
Key Points
  • The word "accept" means to agree to receive or take something, which fits the context of receiving the award.
  • The word "except" means to exclude and does not fit the sentence contextually.
  • "Access" refers to the ability to approach or enter a place, which is unrelated to receiving an award.
  • "Aspect" means a feature or part of something and is not relevant to the given sentence.
Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.
 
Complete Sentence: "He will accept the award at the ceremony tomorrow."

question.en:

question.en:
**Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.**

The writer often used clever ______ to hint at deeper meanings. [MTS, 09 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: “Allusions” are indirect references that hint at something (literature, history, ideas), fitting the context of deeper meanings. “Illusions” are false perceptions; “delusions” are fixed false beliefs; “elusions” is not the intended word here (rare/incorrect in this context). Learning points: allusion ≠ illusion (reference vs false appearance); “to allude to” = to refer indirectly; writers use allusions to add layers of meaning; context clue “hint” strongly signals “allusions”; build vocabulary by common pairs (affect/effect, allusion/illusion).

question.en:

solution.en: “Elude” means to evade/escape capture, which fits the context of avoiding the police. “Allude” means to refer indirectly; “illusion” is a false perception; “allusion” is an indirect reference. question.en: Which sentence has the correct usage? [MTS, 12 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

1.en: He is a man of high council.

2.en: He is a man of high counsel.

3.en: He is a man of high cancel.

4.en: He is a man of high consul.

question.en:

Learning points: (1) adopt = accept/implement; (2) adapt = adjust/change; (3) adept = skilled; (4) common exam trap: adopt vs adapt; (5) collocation: “adopt rules/policy/measure”.

question.en:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The teacher advised him to _____ his mistakes instead of hiding them. [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en:
“Admit” means to acknowledge or confess, which fits the context: admit mistakes. “Admet” is incorrect spelling. “Omit” means leave out/skip, which doesn’t fit. “Admin” is a noun/short form and not appropriate here.
Learning points: (1) Correct collocation: admit a mistake. (2) Grammar: “to + base verb” → “to admit.” (3) Avoid near-looking words: omit vs admit. (4) Spelling trap: admet. (5) Meaning-based completion is safer than guessing.

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one.

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "The truth of the self-conscious individual lies not in its immediate certainty, but in the dialectical movement of its becoming. Consciousness, in its pursuit of knowledge, initially assumes that its object is something external and independent. Yet, through the labor of experience, it discovers that this object is not truly separate but is mediated by consciousness itself. The apparent duality of subject and object is thus sublated in the dialectic, revealing that knowledge is not the passive reception of an external truth but an active process in which consciousness shapes and transforms its own reality. This movement unfolds through a series of contradictions, in which each stage of consciousness, believing itself to have attained certainty, encounters its own inadequacy. The master-slave dialectic exemplifies this: self-consciousness seeks recognition from another, yet in asserting its dominance over the other, it paradoxically undermines its own freedom. The master, in reducing the slave to a mere instrument, deprives himself of a fully realized recognition. Meanwhile, the slave, through labor and self-transformation, attains a deeper awareness of autonomy, demonstrating that freedom is not given but achieved through negation and overcoming.

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "The explanation of a work is always sought in the man or woman who produced it, as if it were always, in the end, through the voice of a single person that literature spoke: through the voice of a single person and the imprints of his or her passions. The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author, his life, his history, and his intentions. But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. This radical displacement shifts the power from the creator to the interpreter, from the supposed intention of the writer to the infinite play of signifiers within the text itself.

question.en:
"The idea that space and time form a four-dimensional continuum was first suggested by Hermann Minkowski as a natural consequence of Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity. In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity."

In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity."

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is based on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Scientists take great pains to defend that assumption, often restricting their vision to the phenomena that the existing paradigm has defined as relevant. When research proceeds in this fashion, findings tend to be incremental, reinforcing the established framework rather than challenging it. Yet, over time, anomalies-empirical observations that cannot be explained within the current paradigm-accumulate. Initially, these anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure. However, as these anomalies grow in number and significance, they begin to erode confidence in the prevailing paradigm. The resolution of such crises is not a straightforward process of falsification, as Popper might suggest, but rather a transformation in the very way scientists see the world. Scientific revolutions occur when a new paradigm emerges-one that is not merely an extension of the old but a fundamental reconceptualization of reality. This shift is not purely logical or empirical; it involves a radical change in perspective, akin to a gestalt switch. The Copernican Revolution, for example, did not merely adjust astronomical calculations; it redefined the very framework through which celestial motion was understood. Similarly, Einstein's theory of relativity did not just modify Newtonian mechanics but replaced its foundational assumptions about space and time.

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: The argument of this book is that we, and all other animals, are machines created by our genes. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived sometimes for millions of years in a highly competitive world. This has entailed ruthless selfishness in gene selection, yet paradoxically it has also favored behaviors that, at an organismal level, may appear cooperative or even altruistic. The key to understanding this paradox lies in recognizing that what matters is not the survival of the individual organism, nor even the species, but rather the continuity of the genes themselves. Natural selection, therefore, operates at the level of replicators-genes-rather than the individual creatures they construct as temporary vehicles. These survival machines, whether they be humans, ants, or oak trees, serve merely as the means through which genes propagate. This gene-centered view of evolution helps explain many otherwise puzzling phenomena in nature. For example, kin selection provides a compelling reason why apparent acts of altruism, such as worker ants sacrificing their ability to reproduce, can evolve: by ensuring the survival and reproduction of closely related individuals, an organism still promotes the continuity of its genetic lineage. This perspective challenges the common anthropocentric tendency to view evolution as a process geared toward the 'good of the species. In reality, natural selection cares nothing for abstract collective welfare; it blindly favors gene variants that are better at replicating, regardless of their consequences beyond that singular goal.

In today's fast-paced world, staying fit and healthy has become more important than ever. Regular exercise helps improve physical strength, mental well-being, and overall energy levels. A combination of cardio exercises, such as running or cycling, and strength training can help keep the body in good shape. Apart from exercise, maintaining a balanced diet plays a crucial role in fitness. Eating fresh fruits, vegetables, and protein-rich foods provides essential nutrients for the body. On the other hand, consuming excessive junk food can lead to health problems like obesity and heart disease. Fitness is not just about physical health; it also impacts mental well-being. Regular workouts release endorphins, which help reduce stress and improve mood. Even simple activities like walking or stretching can make a big difference. Staying fit requires dedication and consistency, but the benefits are worth the effort.

Which of the given options arranges the following sentences in the most logical sequence to form a meaningful paragraph? 1. He believed in non-violent resistance. 2. Mahatma Gandhi was a key figure in India's Freedom Struggle. 3. This set an inspiring example for leaders worldwide. 4. So, he led peaceful protests against British rule.

[Selection Post Phase XIII (10th), 29 Aug 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
The correct logical sequence is **2-1-4-3**.
**1st — 2:** Introduces Mahatma Gandhi as a key figure.
**2nd — 1:** Explains his belief in non-violent resistance.
**3rd — 4:** Result of his belief—he led peaceful protests.
**4th — 3:** Concludes by stating this inspired leaders worldwide.
Correct Answer is **2-1-4-3** because it forms a coherent paragraph.
**Ans: 2-1-4-3**

1.en: Archived manuscripts can seldom being accessed without clearance.

2.en: Archived manuscripts could seldom be accessed without clearance.

3.en: Archived manuscripts can seldom be accessed without clearance.

4.en: Archived manuscripts are seldom able to be accessed without clearance.

solution.en:
**Rule: With modal verbs like 'can', the passive voice is formed using the structure: modal verb + be + past participle (V3).**
The active sentence "People can seldom access..." has 'can' as the modal verb. To convert it to passive, the object 'archived manuscripts' becomes the subject. The verb 'access' changes to 'be accessed' because the modal verb 'can' already conveys the tense and modality.
Option 1 uses 'being', which is incorrect for a simple modal passive.
Option 2 incorrectly uses 'could', changing the meaning from possibility to past possibility.
Option 4 uses 'are able to be', which is unnecessarily wordy and grammatically clumsy in this context.
Correct Answer is **Archived manuscripts can seldom be accessed without clearance** because it correctly uses 'can be accessed' to form the present tense modal passive voice.
**Ans: Archived manuscripts can seldom be accessed without clearance.**

1.en: The office delivers the package every morning.

2.en: Someone delivers the package to the office every morning.

3.en: The office has delivered the package every morning.

4.en: The package delivers itself to the office every morning.

solution.en:
**Rule: To change a sentence from passive voice to active voice, identify the subject performing the action (the agent) and make it the subject of the active sentence. The verb tense must be maintained.**
The passive sentence "The package is delivered..." uses the simple present passive. The implied subject performing the action is 'someone' or a specific person. To make it active, 'someone' or the agent becomes the subject, and the verb changes to 'delivers'.
Option 1 incorrectly makes 'the office' the subject, changing the meaning. Option 3 uses the past perfect, changing the tense. Option 4 uses the present continuous, also changing the tense and meaning.
Correct Answer is **Someone delivers the package to the office every morning** because it correctly identifies the implied subject and maintains the simple present tense.
**Ans: Someone delivers the package to the office every morning.**

1.en: Why have the substantial stylistic anomalies been overlooked by the editor?

2.en: Why are the substantial stylistic anomalies being overlooked by the editor?

3.en: Why did the substantial stylistic anomalies be overlooked by the editor?

4.en: Why were the substantial stylistic anomalies overlooked by the editor?

solution.en:
**Rule: For questions in the simple past tense, the passive voice is formed using 'was/were + past participle'. The question word ('Why') remains at the beginning.**
The active sentence "Why did the editor overlook...?" is in the simple past tense. To convert it to passive, the object 'the substantial stylistic anomalies' becomes the subject. The auxiliary 'did' is replaced by the correct form of 'to be' ('were', because 'anomalies' is plural) and the verb becomes 'overlooked'.
Option 1 incorrectly uses 'have been' (present perfect passive). Option 2 incorrectly uses 'are being' (present continuous passive). Option 3 is grammatically incorrect as it uses 'be' incorrectly after 'did'.
Correct Answer is **Why were the substantial stylistic anomalies overlooked by the editor?** because it correctly uses the simple past passive form 'were overlooked'.
**Ans: Why were the substantial stylistic anomalies overlooked by the editor?**

1.en: Insiders were leaking confidential data within the firm.

2.en: Confidential data had been leaked by insiders, it is alleged.

3.en: Insiders were allegedly leaking confidential data within the firm.

4.en: The firm was allegedly leaking insider data.

solution.en:
**Rule:** In passive-to-active voice, the doer introduced by **'by'** becomes the subject. The tense of the action remains the same.

Here, **'was being leaked by insiders'** is **Past Continuous Passive**:
**was being + V3 (leaked)** → **were + V-ing (leaking)**.

So, **'was being leaked by insiders' → 'insiders were leaking'**. The phrase **'it has been alleged that'** is expressed as **'allegedly'** in the active sentence.

Thus, **Insiders were allegedly leaking confidential data within the firm.**

**Option 3 is correct.**

1.en: The reagents have been double-checked by the laboratory by dawn.

2.en: The reagents will have been double-checked by the laboratory by dawn.

3.en: The reagents will be double-checked by the laboratory by dawn.

4.en: The reagents would have been double-checking by the laboratory by dawn.

solution.en:
**Rule: For the future perfect tense, the passive voice is formed using 'will have been + past participle'.**
The active sentence "The laboratory will have double-checked..." is in the future perfect tense. To convert it to passive, the object 'the reagents' becomes the subject. The verb phrase 'will have double-checked' changes to 'will have been double-checked'.
Option 1 incorrectly uses 'have been', which is present perfect passive. Option 3 uses 'will be', which is simple future passive. Option 4 is grammatically incorrect with 'would have been double-checking'.
Correct Answer is **The reagents will have been double-checked by the laboratory by dawn** because it correctly uses the future perfect passive structure 'will have been double-checked'.
**Ans: The reagents will have been double-checked by the laboratory by dawn.**

1.en: Unauthorized workers extracted the rare minerals before inspection.

2.en: The site was secretly mined before the inspection.

3.en: Unauthorized workers are known to have secretly extracted rare minerals before inspection.

1.en: An external panel has reviewed the proposal.

2.en: The proposal is being reviewed by an external panel.

3.en: They have decided to get the proposal reviewed by an external panel.

4.en: The proposal was reviewed by the panel as per the decision.

solution.en:
**Explanation:**
The given sentence is: **“A decision has been taken to have the proposal reviewed by an external panel.”**

Here, the main passive structure is **“A decision has been taken”**. The doer of this action is not mentioned, so an implied subject such as **“They”** is introduced while converting it into active voice.

**Passive:** A decision **has been taken** to have the proposal reviewed by an external panel.
**Active:** They **have decided** to get the proposal reviewed by an external panel.

In Option 3, **“They have decided”** is the active form of **“A decision has been taken.”** The phrase **“to get the proposal reviewed”** is a **causative construction**. It means that they arranged for the external panel to review the proposal. It does not make the entire sentence a passive-voice answer; the main verb **“have decided”** is active.

Also, **“get + object + past participle”** is a causative structure: **get the proposal reviewed** = **arrange for someone to review the proposal**.

**Why the other options are incorrect:**
• **Option 1:** Changes the meaning. It says the external panel has already reviewed the proposal.
• **Option 2:** **“is being reviewed”** is passive and also changes the tense.
• **Option 4:** **“was reviewed”** is passive and changes the tense/meaning.

Therefore, **Option 3 is correct** because it changes the main passive structure **“A decision has been taken”** into the active structure **“They have decided”**, while retaining the original meaning through the causative expression **“get the proposal reviewed.”**

**Ans: They have decided to get the proposal reviewed by an external panel.**

question.en:
Change the following sentence into the Active form.
It was widely considered that the ancient ruins were believed to have been constructed by a previously unknown civilization.





[CHSL, 29 Nov 2025, Shift 1]

1.en: They widely considered that a previously unknown civilization believed to have constructed the ancient ruins.

2.en: People widely considered that a previously unknown civilization was believed to have constructed the ancient ruins.

3.en: People widely considered that a previously unknown civilization had constructed the ancient ruins.

4.en: It was believed that a previously unknown civilization had constructed the ancient ruins, it was widely considered.

solution.en:
**Rule: To change a passive sentence into active voice, the logical subject of the action is introduced as the subject of the active sentence.**

In the given sentence, **“It was widely considered that the ancient ruins were believed to have been constructed by a previously unknown civilization”**, the passive structure needs to be converted into an active structure.

The phrase **“It was widely considered”** can be changed to **“People widely considered”**. Similarly, **“were believed to have been constructed by a previously unknown civilization”** becomes **“a previously unknown civilization had constructed the ancient ruins.”**

Therefore, the correct active sentence is: **“People widely considered that a previously unknown civilization had constructed the ancient ruins.”**

**Why the other options are incorrect:**
• **Option 1:** “They widely considered...” is grammatically incomplete because **“They”** has no clear antecedent, and the sentence structure is incorrect.
• **Option 2:** “was believed to have been constructed” is still passive, so it does not correctly convert the sentence into active voice.
• **Option 4:** The sentence retains passive construction and also contains incorrect/redundant sentence structure.

Hence, **Option 3 is the correct answer.**
**Ans: People widely considered that a previously unknown civilization had constructed the ancient ruins.**

Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one.

Read the passage and answer the questions: "The truth of the self-conscious individual lies not in its immediate certainty, but in the dialectical movement of its becoming. Consciousness, in its pursuit of knowledge, initially assumes that its object is something external and independent. Yet, through the labor of experience, it discovers that this object is not truly separate but is mediated by consciousness itself. The apparent duality of subject and object is thus sublated in the dialectic, revealing that knowledge is not the passive reception of an external truth but an active process in which consciousness shapes and transforms its own reality. This movement unfolds through a series of contradictions, in which each stage of consciousness, believing itself to have attained certainty, encounters its own inadequacy. The master-slave dialectic exemplifies this: self-consciousness seeks recognition from another, yet in asserting its dominance over the other, it paradoxically undermines its own freedom. The master, in reducing the slave to a mere instrument, deprives himself of a fully realized recognition. Meanwhile, the slave, through labor and self-transformation, attains a deeper awareness of autonomy, demonstrating that freedom is not given but achieved through negation and overcoming.

Read the passage and answer the questions: "The explanation of a work is always sought in the man or woman who produced it, as if it were always, in the end, through the voice of a single person that literature spoke: through the voice of a single person and the imprints of his or her passions. The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author, his life, his history, and his intentions. But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. This radical displacement shifts the power from the creator to the interpreter, from the supposed intention of the writer to the infinite play of signifiers within the text itself.

But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. This radical displacement shifts the power from the creator to the interpreter, from the supposed intention of the writer to the infinite play of signifiers within the text itself.

"The idea that space and time form a four-dimensional continuum was first suggested by Hermann Minkowski as a natural consequence of Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity. In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity."

Read the passage and answer the questions: "Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is based on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Scientists take great pains to defend that assumption, often restricting their vision to the phenomena that the existing paradigm has defined as relevant. When research proceeds in this fashion, findings tend to be incremental, reinforcing the established framework rather than challenging it. Yet, over time, anomalies-empirical observations that cannot be explained within the current paradigm-accumulate. Initially, these anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure. However, as these anomalies grow in number and significance, they begin to erode confidence in the prevailing paradigm. The resolution of such crises is not a straightforward process of falsification, as Popper might suggest, but rather a transformation in the very way scientists see the world. Scientific revolutions occur when a new paradigm emerges-one that is not merely an extension of the old but a fundamental reconceptualization of reality. This shift is not purely logical or empirical; it involves a radical change in perspective, akin to a gestalt switch. The Copernican Revolution, for example, did not merely adjust astronomical calculations; it redefined the very framework through which celestial motion was understood. Similarly, Einstein's theory of relativity did not just modify Newtonian mechanics but replaced its foundational assumptions about space and time.

Read the passage and answer the questions: The argument of this book is that we, and all other animals, are machines created by our genes. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived sometimes for millions of years in a highly competitive world. This has entailed ruthless selfishness in gene selection, yet paradoxically it has also favored behaviors that, at an organismal level, may appear cooperative or even altruistic. The key to understanding this paradox lies in recognizing that what matters is not the survival of the individual organism, nor even the species, but rather the continuity of the genes themselves. Natural selection, therefore, operates at the level of replicators-genes-rather than the individual creatures they construct as temporary vehicles. These survival machines, whether they be humans, ants, or oak trees, serve merely as the means through which genes propagate. This gene-centered view of evolution helps explain many otherwise puzzling phenomena in nature. For example, kin selection provides a compelling reason why apparent acts of altruism, such as worker ants sacrificing their ability to reproduce, can evolve: by ensuring the survival and reproduction of closely related individuals, an organism still promotes the continuity of its genetic lineage. This perspective challenges the common anthropocentric tendency to view evolution as a process geared toward the 'good of the species. In reality, natural selection cares nothing for abstract collective welfare; it blindly favors gene variants that are better at replicating, regardless of their consequences beyond that singular goal.

question.en:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.

"They should have been following the instructions carefully.

[Steno, 07 Aug 2025, Shift 2]

1.en: The instructions should be followed carefully.

2.en: The instructions should have been being followed carefully.

3.en: The instructions should have been followed carefully.

solution.en: The given sentence is in the active voice with a modal verb, perfect aspect, and continuous aspect. The structure is: Subject + should + have + been + V-ing + object. In the passive voice, the object becomes the subject and the continuous form is retained by using 'being' before the past participle (V3). Therefore, 'the instructions' becomes the subject and 'following' changes to 'being followed'. Hence, the correct passive form is: 'The instructions should have been being followed carefully.' Option 3 removes the continuous aspect and therefore is not the exact passive transformation of the given sentence.
solution.hi: दिए गए वाक्य में सहायक क्रिया के साथ पूर्ण तथा निरंतर काल का प्रयोग हुआ है। इसकी रचना है: कर्ता + should + have + been + क्रिया का ing रूप + कर्म। कर्म 'the instructions' को कर्ता के स्थान पर लाकर निरंतरता बनाए रखने के लिए 'being' का प्रयोग किया जाएगा और 'following' का रूप 'being followed' होगा। इसलिए सही कर्मवाच्य वाक्य है: 'The instructions should have been being followed carefully.' विकल्प 3 में निरंतरता समाप्त हो जाती है, इसलिए वह दिए गए वाक्य का सटीक कर्मवाच्य रूप नहीं है।

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one.

Read the passage and answer the questions: "The truth of the self-conscious individual lies not in its immediate certainty, but in the dialectical movement of its becoming. Consciousness, in its pursuit of knowledge, initially assumes that its object is something external and independent. Yet, through the labor of experience, it discovers that this object is not truly separate but is mediated by consciousness itself. The apparent duality of subject and object is thus sublated in the dialectic, revealing that knowledge is not the passive reception of an external truth but an active process in which consciousness shapes and transforms its own reality. This movement unfolds through a series of contradictions, in which each stage of consciousness, believing itself to have attained certainty, encounters its own inadequacy. The master-slave dialectic exemplifies this: self-consciousness seeks recognition from another, yet in asserting its dominance over the other, it paradoxically undermines its own freedom. The master, in reducing the slave to a mere instrument, deprives himself of a fully realized recognition. Meanwhile, the slave, through labor and self-transformation, attains a deeper awareness of autonomy, demonstrating that freedom is not given but achieved through negation and overcoming.

Read the passage and answer the questions: "The explanation of a work is always sought in the man or woman who produced it, as if it were always, in the end, through the voice of a single person that literature spoke: through the voice of a single person and the imprints of his or her passions. The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author, his life, his history, and his intentions. But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. This radical displacement shifts the power from the creator to the interpreter, from the supposed intention of the writer to the infinite play of signifiers within the text itself.

question.en:
"The idea that space and time form a four-dimensional continuum was first suggested by Hermann Minkowski as a natural consequence of Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity. In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity."

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is based on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Scientists take great pains to defend that assumption, often restricting their vision to the phenomena that the existing paradigm has defined as relevant. When research proceeds in this fashion, findings tend to be incremental, reinforcing the established framework rather than challenging it. Yet, over time, anomalies-empirical observations that cannot be explained within the current paradigm-accumulate. Initially, these anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure. However, as these anomalies grow in number and significance, they begin to erode confidence in the prevailing paradigm. The resolution of such crises is not a straightforward process of falsification, as Popper might suggest, but rather a transformation in the very way scientists see the world. Scientific revolutions occur when a new paradigm emerges-one that is not merely an extension of the old but a fundamental reconceptualization of reality. This shift is not purely logical or empirical; it involves a radical change in perspective, akin to a gestalt switch. The Copernican Revolution, for example, did not merely adjust astronomical calculations; it redefined the very framework through which celestial motion was understood. Similarly, Einstein's theory of relativity did not just modify Newtonian mechanics but replaced its foundational assumptions about space and time.

question.en:
Read the passage and answer the questions: The argument of this book is that we, and all other animals, are machines created by our genes. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived sometimes for millions of years in a highly competitive world. This has entailed ruthless selfishness in gene selection, yet paradoxically it has also favored behaviors that, at an organismal level, may appear cooperative or even altruistic. The key to understanding this paradox lies in recognizing that what matters is not the survival of the individual organism, nor even the species, but rather the continuity of the genes themselves. Natural selection, therefore, operates at the level of replicators-genes-rather than the individual creatures they construct as temporary vehicles. These survival machines, whether they be humans, ants, or oak trees, serve merely as the means through which genes propagate. This gene-centered view of evolution helps explain many otherwise puzzling phenomena in nature. For example, kin selection provides a compelling reason why apparent acts of altruism, such as worker ants sacrificing their ability to reproduce, can evolve: by ensuring the survival and reproduction of closely related individuals, an organism still promotes the continuity of its genetic lineage. This perspective challenges the common anthropocentric tendency to view evolution as a process geared toward the 'good of the species. In reality, natural selection cares nothing for abstract collective welfare; it blindly favors gene variants that are better at replicating, regardless of their consequences beyond that singular goal.
