The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. I was an outsider, and, as I had no special matters to air, I was able to spend the evening independently of the others.
A. He was tall, rather thin, very serious, and well dressed.
B. He was the first to attract my attention.
C. There was another gentleman present who like myself had just stumbled upon this affair of domestic bliss.
D. His appearance was not that of a man of birth or high family.
S2. Apparently he had no heart for the family festivities. [MTS, 11 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en: The best sequence is CBDA. After S1, the narrator notes another outsider-like gentleman (C). Then she says he attracted her attention (B). Next she describes his looks (D then A): first a general social impression (not of high birth) (D), then physical description (A). S2 concludes that he had no interest in the festivities. Learning points: (1) Introduce the person before describing (C → B). (2) “He” needs an antecedent—provided by (C). (3) General assessment (D) often precedes detailed description (A). (4) S2 summarises attitude, so it closes well. (5) Maintain narrator perspective and logical progression.

question.en:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Sofia did not raise her eyes from her work, and her slim fingers fairly flew over the delicate lace.
A. She hummed a few bars of a song and recited a verse, but Sofia appeared not to hear.
B. But Lulu wandered about the room, moving the ornaments on the shelves or opening a drawer to gaze absently into it.
C. Then Lulu, who was not blessed with too much patience, decided to put the question boldly, and, planting herself in front of her sister, she asked:
D. It was clear that she wished either to do or to say something but was abashed by her elder sister's grave manner.
S2. "Sofia, do you know what Mademoiselle Jeannette told me?" [MTS, 11 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en: After S1, D logically explains Sofia’s grave manner affecting Lulu. B begins with “But Lulu…” introducing Lulu’s restlessness against Sofia’s focused work. A follows as Lulu tries humming/reciting to get attention. C then shows Lulu finally asking directly, leading into S2 (the question). Learning points: (1) Track contrast markers like “But”; (2) Pronoun/reference continuity (she/her/sister); (3) Look for action escalation: wandering → trying to attract → asking; (4) S2 must follow the “she asked:” cue; (5) Choose the option that places the dialogue trigger immediately before S2.

question.en:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. He remained a day in order to learn the art, because he thought he might be able to turn it to use later on, if by chance he should fail to find other work in Batavia.
A. Neither on the first nor the second day had he realized how lonely he was, because he was captivated by the grand idea of earning enough money to buy two buffaloes, whereas his father had never had more than one, and was too excited over the prospect of seeing Adinda again to grieve over his departure.
B. The following day toward evening he thanked his host and departed.
C. He had left in an anxious hope.
D. As soon as it was dark, and no one could see him, he took out the Melati leaves Adinda had given him, for he was sad, thinking that he would not see her for so long.
S2. The prospect of seeing her again so occupied his heart that on leaving Badoer and passing the tree, he felt something akin to joy, as if the thirty-six moons were already past. [MTS, 11 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en: After S1 (he stayed a day to learn), B naturally gives the departure event next. D then describes what he did at night after departure (Melati leaves; sadness). A reflects on his emotional state across the first/second day and his excitement about seeing Adinda again. C (“He had left in an anxious hope.”) sums up his departure mindset, leading smoothly into S2 about joy at the prospect of meeting her again. Learning points: (1) Time markers: “The following day…” must precede later-night details; (2) Cause-effect linking (departure → night reflection); (3) Emotional arc consistency; (4) Place concluding general sentence near the end; (5) Ensure S2 connects to the final emotional state.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are named A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. She wished she had an hour to visit her old flat in 164th Street - just a turn around the block would be enough, but there wasn't time.
A. "The Prince of Love," she said to herself.
B. An old resentment rose against Honora, who was a born spoilsport and would spoil this trip for her if she could.
C. She walked on, getting her directions, brooding a little because she had been such a city girl once, thinking only of dress and a good time, and now she hardly knew one street from another.
D. She went into the first moving picture theatre she saw because she liked the name of it.
S2. It was about two beautiful young things, a boy with black wavy hair and a girl with curly golden hair, who loved each other and had great troubles, but it all came well in the end, and all the time it was just one fine ballroom or garden after another, and such beautiful clothes! [MTS, 12 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: The sequence BCDA is coherent: after S1, she feels resentment (B) about Honora spoiling the trip; then she continues walking and brooding while taking directions (C); then she enters a moving picture theatre (D); then she reacts to the theatre name with the quote (A), leading naturally into S2 describing what the film was about. Learning points: (1) place emotional reaction sentences (resentment) near the trigger; (2) action progression: walking → entering theatre; (3) quoted line (A) best fits after seeing the theatre name; (4) S2 clearly refers to the movie, so D must precede S2; (5) use “because” clauses (C) as narrative continuation.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are named A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. I knew it was the most famous spot in Honolulu and I entered it with a lively curiosity.
A. It is a large square room, with three entrances, and opposite the bar, which runs the length of it, two corners have been partitioned off into little cubicles.
B. There is a portrait of him, in oils, in a rich gold frame; but there are also two prints of Queen Victoria.
C. Legend states that they were built so that King Kalakaua might drink there without being seen by his subjects, and it is pleasant to think that in one or other of these he may have sat over his bottle, a coal-black potentate, with Robert Louis Stevenson.
D. You get to it by a narrow passage from King Street, and in the passage are offices, so that thirsty souls may be supposed bound for one of these just as well as for the saloon.
S2. On the walls, besides, are old line engravings of the eighteenth century, one of which, and heaven knows how it got there, is after a theatrical picture by de Wilde; and there are oleographs from the Christmas supplements of the Graphic and the Illustrated London News of twenty years ago. [MTS, 12 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: DACB fits: after entering (S1), the narrator explains how you get to it via a narrow passage (D), then describes the room layout (A). Next, “two corners partitioned into cubicles” leads to the legend about why those cubicles existed (C). Finally, details of wall items/portraits (B) smoothly connect to S2 which continues describing engravings and oleographs on the walls. Learning points: (1) route/entry description usually comes before interior description; (2) pronoun reference “they” in C refers to “cubicles” in A; (3) descriptive inventory (B) aligns with S2’s wall-description continuation; (4) check cohesion via referents and logical flow; (5) legends/explanations often follow the object being described.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are named A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. The church was empty and dark.
A. In perfect silence, and with his back turned towards me, he was running over the organ keys with one hand while managing the stops with the other.
B. Far away there gleamed a feeble light, like a faint star in the sky; it was the lamp burning on the high altar.
C. And the organ sounded, but in an indescribable manner.
D. By its flickering light, which only helped to make the deep horror of the shadows the more intense, I saw—I saw—Mother, do not disbelieve it— a man.
S2. It seemed as if each note were a sob somewhere in the metal tube, which vibrated under the pressure of the air compressed within it and gave forth a low, almost imperceptible tone, yet exact and true. [MTS, 12 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: BDAC is logical: after S1, the distant altar lamp is noticed (B). That lamp’s flickering light then enables the narrator to see a man (D). Next comes the detailed action of the man at the organ in silence (A), followed by the statement that the organ sounded in an indescribable manner (C), which leads naturally into S2 describing the quality of each note. Learning points: (1) “By its flickering light” in D refers to the lamp in B; (2) A describes the man’s action, so it should follow D (which introduces him); (3) C is a bridge to S2’s sound-description; (4) maintain sensory sequence: sight → discovery → action → sound; (5) match cause-effect cues (“By its… I saw…”).

The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Tears gushed from his eyes; he drove on at random.
A. The night was tolerably clear.
B. Vladimir drove towards it.
C. He saw, not far off, a little village, consisting of four or five houses.
D. Meanwhile the storm had subsided, the clouds dispersed, and before him lay a level plain covered with a white, undulating carpet.
S2. At the first cottage he jumped out of the sledge, ran to the window and began to knock. [MTS, 12 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en: The logical flow is: after driving randomly (S1), the scene description should set the weather/visibility and terrain (D), then mention the clear night (A), then he spots the village (C), then he drives toward it (B), leading naturally to reaching the first cottage (S2). Hence sequence DACB. Learning points: place setting before action; introduce object (village) before “towards it”; maintain cause-effect; watch pronoun/reference (“it” must have an antecedent).

question.en:

The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Two days and two nights did Peter sleep without once awakening.
A. He looked; there were two bags of gold.
B. When he came to himself, on the third day, he looked long at all the corners of his hut but in vain did he endeavour to recollect what had taken place; his memory was like a miser's pocket from which you cannot entice a quarter of a kopek.
C. Stretching himself, he heard something clash at his feet.
D. Then, only as if in a dream, he recollected that he had been seeking for treasure and that something had frightened him in the woods.
S2. But at what price he had obtained it, and how, he could by no means tell. [MTS, 12 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en: After S1 (he slept), B logically follows (he came to himself on the third day, memory unclear). Then C (he hears something clash at his feet), then A (he sees two bags of gold), then D (he recollects the treasure-seeking in a dreamlike way), leading into S2 (he cannot tell at what price/how he obtained it). Hence BCAD. Learning points: time markers (“on the third day”) should appear early; sensory trigger (clash) precedes discovery (gold); recollection comes after discovery; ensure narrative coherence.

question.en:

S1. Confidence is either a gift or an acquisition.
A. Whenever an opportunity is accepted, opposite effects follow: the fact of acceptance tends to strengthen fain in self, even though the outcome be not altogether satisfactory, provided the will persists to accept other opportunities.
B. Whenever an opportunity is declined because of fear, confidence is weakened; that the lack of it is emphasized in consciousness.

D. In the latter case, it is born of opportunities successfully taken.
S2. Under this method the growth of confidence is not stopped by occasional failures. [MTS, 12 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en: The correct sequence is **D → B → C → A**. After S1 introduces confidence as gift/acquisition, **D** logically explains the “acquisition” route (“In the latter case…”). Then **B** contrasts what happens when opportunities are declined (fear weakens confidence). **C** follows B by explaining the psychological effect (“Either vibrations are induced…”), and **A** completes the contrast by describing the positive effect when opportunities are accepted, which leads smoothly into S2’s conclusion about growth despite occasional failures. Learning points: (1) look for linkers like “in the latter case,” (2) maintain contrast pairs: declined vs accepted, (3) ensure pronoun/connector references are resolved, (4) place general-to-specific and cause-to-effect logically.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. After the repast, play is proposed.
A. A dispute arises on some circumstances in the game, and the disputants grow warm one of his intimate friends throws a dice box at his head and strikes out one of his eyes.
B. A little play with one's intimate friends is a harmless pastime.
C. The philosopher Mennon is carried home to his house, dark and penniless, with the loss of an eye.
D. He plays and loses all that is in his purse, and four times as much on his word.
S2. He sleeps out his debauch, and when his head has got a little clear, he sends his servant to the Receiver General of the finances of Nineveh to draw a little money to pay his debts of honour to his intimate friends. [MTS, 12 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en: **B → D → A → C** fits best. After S1 (play is proposed), **B** gives a general comment about playing with friends. **D** then narrates what happens: he plays and loses money. **A** escalates the events into a dispute and injury. **C** logically follows as the consequence: he is carried home injured, dark and penniless. This sets up S2, where he later clears his head and arranges money to pay debts. Learning points: (1) arrange events chronologically, (2) place general statement before specific incident, (3) ensure cause (dispute/injury) precedes result (carried home), (4) watch for coherence with S2’s “debts of honour.”

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Having thus laid his little plan of philosophy in his closet, Menon put his head out of the window.
A. The one was old, and appeared quite at her ease.
B. The other was young, handsome, and seemingly much agitated: she sighed, she wept, and seemed on that account still more beautiful.
C. Our philosopher was touched, not, to be sure, with the beauty of the lady (he was too much determined not to feel any uneasiness of that kind) but with the distress which he saw her in.
D. He saw two women walking under the plane trees near his house.
S2. He came downstairs and accosted the young Ninevite in the design of consoling her with philosophy. [MTS, 13 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: After S1 (he looks out of the window), it logically follows that he **sees two women** (D). Then the description naturally splits into “the one” (old) (A) and “the other” (young and agitated) (B). After observing their state, the philosopher is moved by her distress (C), which leads coherently to S2 where he comes downstairs to console the young woman. Learning points: pronoun/connector cues (“the one…the other”) fix A and B order; observation precedes reaction; maintain character continuity (young Ninevite in S2 aligns with “the other” in B).

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. What a night!
A. Alas, how shall we paint the emotions that arose in her soul, that divided, tore it between love and virtue?
B. What a dreadful night for Lydia!
C. They led her to the altar as it were to punishment.
D. She adored Lausua, she detested Mezentius, she was sacrificing herself to her father's interests, delivering herself up to the object of her hatred, tearing herself forever from an adored lover.
S2. Barbarous Mezentius! Thou art content to reign over the heart by violence and fear! [MTS, 13 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: S1 sets an exclamatory tone. Next, specifying whose night it was (“for Lydia”) (B) is natural. Then the text explores her inner conflict/emotions (A), followed by the detailed explanation of her situation (D). Finally, the narrative moves to the action of being led to the altar (C), which connects to the condemnation of Mezentius in S2. Learning points: general → specific flow; emotion framing often precedes detailed circumstances; action (“led her to the altar”) fits after explaining why it feels like punishment.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. I do not believe that chickens await the hour when the housewife brings their corn with as much anxiety as Peter awaited the evening.
A. How long it was!
B. But now the sun has set.
C. Evidently God's day had lost its end somewhere.
D. He kept looking to see whether the shadows of the trees were not lengthening, whether the sun was not turning red towards setting; and, the longer he watched, the more impatient he grew.
S2. The sky is red only on one side, and it is already growing dark. [MTS, 13 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: After S1 (Peter anxiously awaited evening), the next logical sentence is his repeated watching of the setting signs (D). Then his impatience is summarized (“How long it was!”) (A). Next, the narrator comments on the unusual delay (“God's day had lost its end…”) (C). Then the transition “But now the sun has set” (B) leads smoothly into S2 describing the sky and darkness. Learning points: keep cause → reaction order; “But now” signals a late-stage transition, so B must come near the end; descriptive continuity with sunset/dark in S2 supports B right before S2.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence, keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.'
A. Christ, the special manifestation of the Absolute is known and knowable.
B. The Word has two manifestations—the general one of Nature and the special one of the great Incarnations of God: Krishna, Buddha, Jesus and Ramakrishna.
C. The Hindu calls this maya, the manifestation of God, because it is the power of God.
D. The Absolute reflecting through the universe is what we call Nature.
S2. The Absolute cannot be known; We cannot know the Father, only the Son. [MTS, 13 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en: The coherent flow is: after S1 introduces “the Word,” C introduces the Hindu concept of maya as God’s manifestation, D defines Nature as the Absolute reflected through the universe, B then explains the two manifestations (general Nature and special incarnations), and A narrows to Christ as the special manifestation that is knowable, leading naturally into S2 (“only the Son”). Hence the correct sequence is C–D–B–A. Learning points: (1) Use definitional links (Nature ↔ Absolute) to order; (2) move from general concept to specific example; (3) pronoun/reference tracking (“this” in C needs an antecedent idea of manifestation); (4) concluding sentence S2 aligns with “Son/Christ” just before it; (5) keep thematic progression (Word → manifestation → Nature/incarnations → Christ).

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. At last Vladimir perceived that he was going in the wrong direction.
A. His horse could scarcely move forward.
B. He turned to the right now.
C. He had now been on the road for more than an hour.
D. He stopped, began to think, to recollect, and compare, and he felt convinced that he ought to have turned to the right.
S2. Jadrino could not be far off. [MTS, 13 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en: After S1 (realising he is wrong), D logically follows: he stops and thinks and becomes convinced he should have turned right; then B shows the corrective action (he turns right). The remaining details can then follow to sustain narration: A (horse could scarcely move forward) adds difficulty in progress, and C gives the time reference (“more than an hour”), culminating in S2 (destination not far). Thus the best sequence among the options is D–B–A–C. Learning points: (1) Cause → reflection → action is a common narrative order; (2) D contains the decision, so it must precede B (action); (3) descriptive details (horse/time) often come after the turning point; (4) S2 is a concluding inference, so it stays last; (5) in ordering, look for “now” indicating immediate next action.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. I'm doing fine, except I've got no appetite.
A. I keep hearing: "Goodness, you look awful!"
B. The atmosphere is stifling, sluggish, leaden.
C. My nerves often get the better of me, especially on Sundays; that is when I really feel miserable.
D. I must admit they're doing their best to keep me in condition: they're plying me with dextrose, cod-liver oil, brewer's yeast and calcium.
S2. Outside, you don't hear a single bird, and a deathly, oppressive silence hangs over the house and clings to me as if it were going to drag me into the deepest regions of the underworld. [MTS, 13 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en: The logical flow is S1 → A → D → C → B → S2. After S1 (no appetite), A introduces what others say (“you look awful!”), D explains the care being given (dextrose, cod-liver oil, etc.), C describes the speaker’s nerves and Sunday misery, and B sets the heavy atmospheric tone leading into S2’s deathly silence outside. Learning points: (1) Look for cause–effect and topic flow. (2) Pronoun/reference links guide order. (3) Mood-building sentences usually come just before atmospheric closing. (4) Eliminate options that break coherence between A, D, C, B.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. In front of this building, overlooking the river, is a garden, where the once well-trimmed box borders that used to define the walks now grow wild as they list.
A. The rich vegetation of those weeds that we call foul adorns the sloping shore.
B. The wall fruit grows like hedges against the walls.
C. Several willows that spring from the Loire have grown as rapidly as the hedge that encloses it and half conceal the house.
D. Fruit trees, neglected for the last ten years, no longer yield their harvest, and their shoots form coppices.
S2. Paths once gravelled are overgrown with moss, but to tell the truth, there is no trace of a path. [MTS, 13 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en: The logical sequence is S1 → C → A → D → B → S2. After S1 (wild garden by river), C introduces willows from the Loire half-concealing the house, A describes the rich weed vegetation on the sloping shore, D notes neglected fruit trees forming coppices, and B adds wall fruit growing like hedges, before S2 closes with overgrown paths. Learning points: (1) Use geography (river → shore → trees → walls) to track flow. (2) Specific images often follow general scene. (3) Look for natural progression of description. (4) Eliminate options that disturb visual logic.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. When the short days of winter came, dusk fell before we had well eaten our dinners.
A. Our shouts echoed in the silent street.
B. When we met in the street the houses had grown sombre.
C. The space of sky above us was the colour of ever-changing violet and towards it the lamps of the street lifted their feeble lanterns.
D. The cold air stung us and we played till our bodies glowed.
S2. The career of our play brought us through dark muddy lanes behind the houses, where we ran the gauntlet of the rough tribes from the cottages, to the back doors of the dark dripping gardens where odours arose from the ashpits, to the dark odorous stables where a coachman smoothed and combed the horse or shook music from the buckled harness. [MTS, 16 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: After S1 sets the winter-evening scene, B logically follows (meeting in the street; houses look sombre). Then C describes the sky and street lamps, expanding the dusk imagery. D fits next as it describes playing in the cold air. A (“Our shouts echoed…”) naturally follows the playing/action before S2’s extended description of where their play took them. Learning points: (1) Identify scene-setting (S1) and concluding movement (S2). (2) Use connectors like time/setting → description → action → sound/result. (3) Look for pronoun/idea continuity (“we met,” “we played,” “our shouts”). (4) In para-jumbles, sensory description often precedes action-based sentences.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. There, for the first time, had the painter caught sight of Laurella who, with her pitcher on her head, had passed by without taking any notice of him.
A. A very ungentle ball came knocking against his shins as a reminder that this was not the spot to choose for meditation.
B. But the young boatman who had thrown the ball stood silent among his friends, in such an attitude of defiance that the stranger had found it more advisable to go his way and avoid discussion.
C. The Neapolitan, struck by her appearance, stood still and gazed after her, not heeding that he was standing in the very midst of the game, which, with two steps, he might have cleared.
D. He looked round, as if in expectation of some excuse.
S2. Still, this little encounter had been spoken of, particularly at the time when the painter had been pressing his suit to Laurella. [MTS, 16 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en: After S1 introduces Laurella and the painter noticing her, C naturally follows by explaining his reaction (he stands still, gazing). Then A occurs as a consequence (a ball hits his shins because he is in the middle of the game). D follows as his immediate response (he looks around, expecting an excuse). Finally B completes the encounter by describing the boatman’s defiant stance and why the stranger leaves, leading smoothly to S2 referencing how the encounter was later discussed. Learning points: (1) Cause-effect ordering is crucial (gazing → gets hit by ball). (2) “He looked round” must follow an incident prompting it. (3) “But” in B signals contrast and fits after the situation is established. (4) Match character references consistently (painter/Neapolitan/stranger).

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Down in the dust though my spirit was, I might have tried to strike him for those words if at that moment I had not noticed something very surprising.
A. When, therefore, Mr. Preston gave me the coat which he had picked up from the floor, I saw with terror that my own was already hanging on my arm and that the two were alike in every way.
B. My coat had cost more money than most men could spend, and it had been made especially for me.
C. I remembered that the strange being who had so mysteriously entered and left the room had had a coat.
D. It was different, I thought, from every other coat in the world.
S2. No one else in the group had been wearing one. [MTS, 16 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en: The correct sequence is BDAC. First, B introduces the coat’s cost/special making; D follows naturally stating it was unique; A then presents the surprise of two identical coats (his own already on his arm); C then recalls the mysterious being had a coat, setting up S2 that no one else wore one. Learning points: (1) Look for pronoun/reference links (“it,” “the coat”). (2) “Therefore” in A indicates it follows earlier context about the coat. (3) Unique → shock at identical is a logical progression. (4) End sentence S2 must be supported by the recall in C.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. You can testify that I was never a coward.
A. All my life long, in Jaen, in Madrid, and elsewhere, I have walked the streets at all hours, alone and unarmed, and if I have chanced to run upon suspicious-looking persons, thieves, or mere sneaking beggars, they have had to get out of my way or take to their heels.
B. I fought a dupl once, when I had to, like any other man.
C. But if the person turned out to be a solitary woman, standing still or walking, and I was also alone, with no one in sight in any direction, then (laugh) if you want to, but believe me) I would be all covered over with goose-flesh; vague fears would assail me; I would think about beings of the other world, about imaginary existences, and about all the superstitious stories which would make me laugh under other circumstances.
D. Just after I had left the School of Engineers, my workmen in Despeafierros revolted, and I fought them with stick and pistol until I made them submit.
S2. I would quicken my pace, or else turn back, and would not get over my fright in the least until safe in my own house. [MTS, 16 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en: The correct order is BDAC. B provides a general brave act (a duel); D adds another strong example (fighting revolting workmen), supporting S1. A then broadens the claim with habitual fearlessness in streets. C introduces the contrast (“But…”) revealing his irrational fear when encountering a solitary woman, which leads logically to S2 about quickening pace/turning back until safe. Learning points: (1) “But” in C signals a turning point after examples of bravery. (2) Arrange from general claim → supporting examples → contrast. (3) Time marker “Just after…” in D fits early-life evidence. (4) S2 must follow the “fear” situation in C.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. An enormous lion advances.
A. Terror and pity seize on every breast.
B. In a short time, the sound of clarions animates him; he replies by his roarings; his shaggy mane is erected around his monstrous head; he lashes his loins with his tail, and the fire begins to issue from his sparkling eyeballs.
C. At first, with a calm pride, he traverses the arena, throwing his dreadful looks round the amphitheatre that environs him; a confused murmur announces the terror that he inspires.
D. The affrighted populace wish and dread to see the wretch appear who is to be delivered up to the rage of this monster.
S2. The combatant, whom Mezentius' guards themselves had taken for Phanor, presents himself. [MTS, 16 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en: The sequence CBDA is coherent. C describes the lion’s initial movement in the arena; B then intensifies the description as sounds excite him; D shifts to the crowd’s anticipation of the victim/combatant; A captures the crowd’s emotions (terror and pity) before S2 introduces the combatant who finally appears. Learning points: (1) “At first” in C indicates an early position. (2) B continues physical description logically after C. (3) Crowd-focused sentences (D, A) should precede the arrival in S2. (4) Maintain narrative flow: lion → escalation → crowd reaction → entry of combatant.

question.en:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. He was older than I.
A. But his strange, heavy, almost waxen face was not lined by experience.
B. And sometimes that face, in stillness when he listened to me playing, with the heavy eyelids folded over eyes that always disturbed me by their absolute absence of light, seemed to me like a mask, as if his real face, the face that truly reflected all the life he had led in the world before he met me, before, even, I was born, as though that face lay underneath this mask.
C. Rather, experience seemed to have washed it perfectly smooth, like a stone on a beach whose fissures have been eroded by successive tides.
D. He was much older than I; there were streaks of pure silver in his dark mane.
S2. Or else, elsewhere.
[MTS, 16 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
The correct sequence is DACB.
- S1 establishes that the subject is older than the narrator.
- D reinforces and expands on this age difference with concrete physical evidence ("streaks of pure silver in his dark mane").
- A introduces a contrast using "But," noting that despite his age, his face was surprisingly unlined by experience.
- C follows naturally from A with "Rather," providing the explanation for why his face appeared unlined—it had been smoothed by experience like a stone eroded by tides.
- B develops the description further, exploring the mask-like quality of this smooth, expressionless face.
- S2 concludes with an enigmatic suggestion that his true self exists somewhere hidden or elsewhere.
This sequence creates a smooth progression from general observation of age → physical evidence → description of face → explanation of appearance → deeper reflection on hidden nature.

question.en:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. It was a blazing hot day in August.
A. For myself, my term of service in India had trained me to stand heat better than cold, and a thermometer at ninety was no hardship.
B. Our blinds were half drawn, and Holmes lay curled upon the sofa, reading and re-reading a letter which he had received by the morning post.
C. Baker Street was like an oven, and the glare of the sunlight upon the yellow brickwork of the house across the road was painful to the eye.
D. It was hard to believe that these were the same walls which loomed so gloomily through the fogs of winter.
S2. But the morning paper was uninteresting.
[MTS, 16 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
The sequence CDBA follows a logical narrative flow.
- S1 establishes the setting: a blazing hot August day.
- C expands on the heat's impact on Baker Street specifically, describing it as "like an oven" with painful glare on the brickwork—moving from general weather to specific location.
- D provides a contrasting reflection, comparing the current bright, harsh scene with the gloomy winter appearance of the same walls.
- B shifts focus from outside to inside, describing the indoor scene with Holmes on the sofa and half-drawn blinds (a response to the heat).
- A presents the narrator's personal perspective on the heat, explaining his tolerance for it due to his Indian service.
- S2 transitions to a new topic (the morning paper), connected by "But" to shift from the heat discussion.
This creates a camera-like movement: weather → street outside → contrast with winter → inside the room → narrator's reaction → shift to new topic.

question.en:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Jovinian, however, having quitted the water, sought in every possible direction for his horse and clothes and, to his utter astonishment, could find neither.
A. "Miserable man that I am," said he, "to what a strait am I reduced!
B. I will then ride on to the palace and strictly investigate the cause of this extraordinary conduct.
C. There is, I remember, a knight who lives close by; I will go to him and command his attendance and service.
D. Vexed beyond measure at the circumstance (for he was completely naked and saw no one near to assist him), he began to reflect upon what course he should pursue.
S2. Some shall smart for it."
[MTS, 16 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
The correct sequence is DACB, which follows a clear emotional and logical progression.
- S1 introduces the situation: Jovinian has come out of the water and cannot find his horse or clothes.
- D comes next because it explains his immediate condition and reaction: he is completely naked, helpless, and begins to think about what he should do.
- A naturally follows D as his first emotional response after reflecting on his miserable condition. He cries out, “Miserable man that I am...”
- C then gives the practical solution he thinks of: he remembers a nearby knight and decides to go to him for assistance and service.
- B follows C because after getting help from the knight, he plans to ride to the palace and investigate the strange conduct.
- S2 completes the thought with his angry threat: “Some shall smart for it.”
Thus, the logical order is: S1 → D → A → C → B → S2.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. From beyond the sea came hosts of Greeks, armed for war and bent upon the conquest of the city.
A. The cry was for vengeance, and heroes and warriors from every city and town joined hands and vowed vengeance upon Troy.
B. He had stolen and carried away from her shores the most beautiful of all her women, even Helen, the wife of Menelaus of Sparta.
C. They came in a thousand little ships, with sails and oars, and landed on the beach at the foot of the plain.
D. They came because one of the princes of Troy, Paris by name, had done a grievous wrong to Greece.
S2. They built huts and tents along the shore; they kindled fires; they threw up a breastwork of earth and stones around their camp; they defied the warriors of Troy to come out on the plain and meet them in battle. [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en:
The logical flow is: reason first (D: why they came), then the specific wrong (B: Helen’s abduction), then the wider response (A: Greeks vow vengeance), then the arrival details (C: ships and landing), leading into S2 (camp built). Hence DBAC.
Learning points: (1) Coherence often follows: cause → detail → reaction → action. (2) Pronoun tracking: “He” in B refers back to Paris introduced in D. (3) Broad-to-specific sequencing helps. (4) S2 continues naturally after landing (C). (5) Look for dependency links (Paris → He).

The other four sentences between first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. As for Simmons, he, it was held, was fortunate in that capable wife.
A. Nobody could tell what might not have happened to Tommy Simmons if there had been no Mrs. Simmons to take care of him.
B. He had no vices (even his pipe departed him after his marriage), and Mrs. Simmons had ingrained on him divers exotic virtues.
C. He was a moderately good carpenter and joiner, but no man of the world, and he wanted to be one.
D. He was a meek and quiet man, with a boyish face and sparse, limp whiskers.
S2. He went solemnly to chapel every Sunday, under a tall hat, and put a penny - one returned to him for the purpose out of his week's wages - in the plate. [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en:
After S1 (fortunate because of his wife), it makes sense to describe Simmons (C: his limited worldliness), then his appearance/temperament (A? actually D fits better before A), then D (meek, quiet, boyish face), then A (what might have happened without Mrs. Simmons), and then B (no vices; wife ingrained virtues), leading to S2 (chapel routine). The option matching the intended coherence is CADB.
Learning points: (1) Build from general claim to supporting details. (2) Character description (C, D) usually precedes consequences (A). (3) Wife’s influence is reinforced in A and B. (4) S2 is an example of his virtuous routine. (5) Look for narrative escalation: trait → dependence → reform.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. It was a close, musty, ill-ventilated place, as might be expected, since its inmate seldom left it.
A. A thick dark veil covered her face, but it was cut off close at her upper lip and disclosed a perfectly shaped mouth and a delicately rounded chin.
B. From keeping beasts in a cage, the woman seemed, by some retribution of fate, to have become herself a beast in a cage.
C. She sat now in a broken armchair in the shadowy corner of the room.
D. Long years of inaction had coarsened the lines of her figure, but at some period it must have been beautiful, and was still full and voluptuous.
S2. I could well conceive that she had indeed been a very remarkable woman. [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en:
The best sequence is BCDA: after describing the place (S1), the text logically introduces the woman’s caged condition (B), then her position in the room (C), then her veiled face details (A), followed by her figure description (D), and concludes with the overall impression (S2).

Why other options are wrong: Other orders break the flow from general description → position → facial details → figure details → concluding remark.

Learning points: (1) Move from general setting to the subject. (2) Keep physical positioning before close-up description. (3) Maintain descriptive coherence (face/figure). (4) Ensure smooth link to the concluding sentence. (5) Look for logical zoom-in: room → person → details.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. The two went to their business.
A. he seated himself at the matchmaker’s side but facing him, attempting by an act of will to suppress the unpleasant tickle in his throat.
B. As he flipped through them, a gesture and sound that physically hurt Leo, the student pretended not to see and gazed steadfastly out the window.
C. Salzman eagerly unstrapped his portfolio and removed a loose rubber band from a thin packet of much-handled cards.
D. Leo had led Salzman to the only clear place in the room, a table near a window that overlooked the lamp-lit city.
S2. Although it was still February, winter was on its last legs, signs of which he had for the first time in years begun to notice. [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en:
The best order is DACB: they begin the task (S1), then Leo leads Salzman to the table (D), Leo sits and composes himself (A), Salzman takes out the cards (C), and then flips through them while Leo looks away (B), before the reflective close (S2).

Why other options are wrong: Alternative sequences place actions (cards/flipping) before the scene is set at the table/window or disrupt the cause-effect flow of actions.

Learning points: (1) Establish location before actions with objects. (2) Follow chronological action: lead → sit → take out → flip through. (3) Pronoun references (“he”) must have a clear antecedent. (4) Maintain smooth narrative progression. (5) End with the reflective/atmospheric sentence.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. On the morning of the fourth day, while Khaled, according to his custom, rode out over the plain and passed close to the tents reserved for strangers, he caught sight of Djaidat mounting her horse.
A. At this moment I have failed in courtesy towards you, but I now beg of you, in the name of that God who has given you such great dexterity in arms, tell me who you are, and to what noble princes are you allied?
B. He saluted her, and she returned his salute.
C. For I have never met your equal amongst brave warriors.
D. "Noble Arab," said Khaled, "I would ask you one question."
S2. Answer me, I beseech you, for I am most impatient to learn." [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en:
The best sequence is BDAC: after Khaled sees her (S1), they exchange salutes (B), then he begins speaking (D), explains his admiration (A) and supports it with praise (C), and finally urges an answer (S2).

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences place the question/praise before the greeting/salute or disrupt the natural flow of dialogue (opening → request → compliment → insistence).

Learning points: (1) Dialogue usually follows greeting/action first. (2) “said Khaled” introduces his speech early. (3) Praise often supports a request. (4) End aligns with “Answer me…” (S2). (5) Maintain conversational logic.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Miss Janet Dalrymple, daughter of the first Lord Stair and Dame Margaret Ross, had engaged herself without the knowledge of her parents to the Lord Rutherford, who was not acceptable to them either on account of his political principles or his want of fortune.
A. The young lady refused the proposal and being pressed on the subject, confessed her secret engagement.
B. Shortly after, a suitor who was favoured by Lord Stair, and still more so by his lady, paid his addresses to Miss Dalrymple.
C. Lady Stair, a woman accustomed to universal submission (or even her husband did not dare to contradict her), treated this objection as a trifle and insisted upon her daughter yielding her consent to marry the new suitor, David Dunbar, son and heir to David Dunbar of Baldoon, in Wigtownshire.
D. The young couple broke a piece of gold together and pledged their troth in the most solemn manner, and it is said the young lady imprecated dreadful evils on herself should she break her plighted faith.
S2. The first lover, a man of very high spirit, then interfered by letter and insisted on the right he had acquired by his troth plighted with the young lady. [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
The correct sequence is DBAC: after the engagement is mentioned (S1), the solemn pledge is described (D), then the favoured suitor appears (B), the girl refuses and confesses (A), and Lady Stair forces the new match (C), leading to the lover’s letter (S2).

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences misplace the background pledge (D) or put Lady Stair’s insistence (C) before the refusal/confession (A), breaking cause-effect flow.

Learning points: (1) Place background/details near the event they explain. (2) Track cause → reaction → consequence. (3) Identify “trigger” actions (proposal, refusal, insistence). (4) Keep pronoun/reference clarity (who objected/insisted). (5) S1/S2 provide the frame—fit the middle accordingly.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Menon, covered with shame and confusion, got home to his own house; there he found a card inviting him to dinner with some of his intimate friends.
A. I shall forget in the sweets of their society that folly I have this morning been guilty of.
B. Accordingly, he attends the meeting; he is discovered to be uneasy at something, and he is urged to drink and banish care.
C. It will therefore be prudent in me to go to my intimate friends and partake with them of a frugal repast.
D. If I remain at home alone, said he, I shall have my mind so occupied with this vexatious adventure that I shall not be able to eat a bit, and shall bring upon myself some disease.
S2. A little wine, drunk in moderation, comforts the heart of god and man; so, reasons Menon the philosopher, and he becomes intoxicated. [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
The correct sequence is DCAB: D gives Menon’s reasoning to avoid staying alone, C follows with the decision to go to friends, A adds his intention to forget his folly in their company, and B then narrates what happens at the meeting, leading into S2.

Why other options are wrong: Other orders place “accordingly” (B) too early or break the logical chain from reason (D) → decision (C) → intention (A) → action/result (B).

Learning points: (1) “Accordingly” signals a result/action after a decision. (2) Reasons usually precede decisions. (3) Look for connectors like “therefore” that demand prior context. (4) Keep timeline: home → decision → meeting → drinking. (5) S2 is the outcome; place drinking-related build-up right before it.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. My two old gentlemen sat half in the shadow of the green lamp-shade, moldering ruins both, from long past days, bowed and dim, gazing before them with the dull glance of the dimming eyes of age.
A. One, the host, is evidently an old officer, as you would recognize at once from his carefully wound cravat, his pointed, sharply cut mustache, and his martial eyebrows.
B. The other, who sits near him on the sofa, a tall, spare figure, his narrow shoulders crowned by the high-domed head of a thinker, draws occasionally thin puffs of smoke from a long pipe which is just about to go out.
C. He sits holding the handle of his roller-chair like a crutch tightly clasped in both hands.
D. Among the myriad wrinkles of his smooth-shaven, dried-up face, framed in a wreath of snow-white curls, there lurked a quiet, gentle smile, a smile which the peace of resignation alone can bring to the face of age.
S2. He is motionless except for his jaws, which move up and down ceaselessly with the motion of chewing. [MTS, 17 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
The correct sequence is ACDB: after the general description (S1), A identifies the host, C describes his posture with the roller-chair, D details his facial expression, and B then describes the other gentleman, ending with S2 about his motionless chewing.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences introduce “the other” (B) too early or separate closely linked details about the host (A, C, D), reducing coherence.

Learning points: (1) Move from general to specific. (2) Keep descriptions of the same person together. (3) “One…the other…” structure usually follows in order. (4) Physical posture details often follow identification. (5) End with a closing action/observation that matches S2.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Ash's books were most regrettably scattered across Europe and America.
A. That was no problem nowadays, books travelled the aether like light and sound.
B. And Roland was looking for sources for Ash's Garden of Proserpine.
C. But it was just possible that Ash's own Vico had marginalia missed even by the indefatigable Cropper.
D. By far the largest single gathering was of course in the Stant Collection at Robert Dale Owen University in New Mexico, where Mortimer Cropper worked on his monumental edition of the Complete Correspondence of Randolph Henry Ash.
S2. And there was a pleasure to be had from reading the sentences Ash had read, touched with his fingers, scanned with his eyes. [MTS, 18 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en:
The best sequence is DACB: after S1 (books scattered), D logically adds where the largest collection was; A follows with “That was no problem nowadays…” referring to accessing books; C adds a contrast (“But it was just possible…”) about marginalia; B then mentions Roland’s specific search, leading naturally to S2 about pleasure in reading what Ash read.

Why other options are wrong: Other orders break reference links like “That” (A) and “But” (C) or place Roland’s search (B) before establishing the collections/access context.

Learning points: (1) Track pronoun/reference words: “That,” “But,” “And.” (2) Place general setting before specifics. (3) Contrast markers (“But”) usually follow a prior statement. (4) “And Roland…” fits after context is set. (5) Ensure S2 feels like a concluding reflection.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. He saw a most wonderful sight.
A. In every tree that he could see there was a little child.
B. The birds were flying about and twittering with delight, and the flowers were looking up through the green grass and laughing.
C. And the trees were so glad to have the children back again that they covered themselves with blossoms and were waving their arms gently above the children's heads.
D. Through a little hole in the wall the children had crept in, and they were sitting in the branches of the trees.
S2. It was a lovely scene, only in one corner it was still winter. [MTS, 18 Feb 2025, Shift 1]

solution.en:
The sequence DACB is coherent: D explains how the children entered and where they were; A generalises the sight (children in every tree); C shows the trees’ joyful reaction; B broadens the scene with birds/flowers, leading smoothly to S2’s concluding contrast about winter in one corner.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences place descriptive reactions (C/B) before establishing how/where the children are (D), weakening the narrative flow from cause to description to conclusion.

Learning points: (1) Establish setting/action first (entry via hole). (2) Then general description (“in every tree”). (3) Reactions/consequences follow (trees glad). (4) Wider scenic details often come later (birds/flowers). (5) End with a summary/contrast sentence (S2).

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. The sailor took home his gold, made his ship ready, and then, taking leave of his wife and sons, he went down to the shore, where he found the old man waiting for him with a slave and twenty ass-loads of empty sacks. Abu'l Fawaris greeted him, and together they loaded the ship and set sail.
A. For this the old man steered, and they soon landed upon it.
B. This they reached after some hours of travel and climbed to the summit, upon which they found a broad plain where more than two hundred pits had been dug.
C. Having loaded his slave with some sacks, the old man with his companions set out towards a mountain which they could see in the distance.
D. Taking a particular star for their mark, they sailed for three months, when an island appeared to one side of them.
S2. The old man then explained to the sailor that he was a merchant and that he had, on that spot, found a mine of jewels. [MTS, 18 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en:
The sequence DACB maintains narrative order: first they sail and spot an island (D), then steer to it and land (A), then head toward a mountain (C), and finally reach the summit and find pits (B), leading into S2 about a mine of jewels.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences misplace “landed upon it” before the island appears, or place the mountain journey before reaching the island, breaking cause-effect flow.

Learning points: (1) Track travel stages: sail → island appears → land → move inland → reach summit. (2) Pronouns like “this/it” need clear antecedents. (3) Look for time markers (“sailed for three months”, “soon landed”, “after some hours”). (4) Ensure logical geography progression. (5) S2 should be supported by “pits/mine” just before it.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. And addressing another eunuch, he said to him, O my chief, as thou hopest for Allah's protection, tell me, am I the Prince of the Faithful?
A. And Abou Hassan, perplexed at all that he beheld, said, In one night do I become Prince of the Faithful!
B. He remained perplexed and confounded until the morning, when a eunuch advanced to him and said to him, May Allah grant a happy morning to the Prince of the Faithful!
C. Yea, by Allah, answered the eunuch; thou art at this present time the Prince of the Faithful and the caliph of the Lord of all creatures.
D. Was I not yesterday Abou Hassan, and today am I the Prince of the Faithful?
S2. And he handed to him a pair of shoes of gold stuff, reticulated with precious stones and rubies; and Abou Hassan took them, and after examining them a long time, put them into his sleeve. [MTS, 18 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en:
CADB fits best: after S1’s question, the eunuch confirms he is the Prince (C), then Abou Hassan reacts in amazement (A), then he expresses the yesterday/today contrast (D), and finally the morning scene of being greeted as Prince (B) aligns with his continued perplexity before S2’s gift episode.

Why other options are wrong: Sequences placing (B) too early disrupt the direct question–answer exchange in S1; others misplace the reaction lines (A/D) away from the confirmation (C).

Learning points: (1) Dialogue pairs: question → answer should stay together. (2) Reaction statements follow the confirmation. (3) Time cues (“until the morning”) usually come after initial night confusion. (4) Keep coherence of speaker and scene. (5) Ensure S2 follows a settled “Prince” setting.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Saidjah, who was then about seven, soon made friends with the new buffalo.
A. Such a friendship the little Saidjah had soon been able to make with the newcomer; and it seemed as if the encouraging voice of the child gave more strength to the heavy shoulders of the animal, when it tore open the stiff clay and traced its way in deep sharp furrows.
B. Of this attachment I shall soon give an example.
C. The large strong animal bends its heavy head to the right, to the left, or downwards, just as the pressure of the child's finger directs.
D. I purposely say “made friends,” for it was indeed touching to see how the buffalo was attached to the little boy who watched over and fed him.
S2. The buffalo turned willingly on reaching the end of the field, not losing an inch of ground when plowing backwards the new furrow, which was ever near the old, as if the sawah was a garden ground raked by a giant. [MTS, 18 Feb 2025, Shift 2]

solution.en:
DBCA is coherent: the narrator clarifies “made friends” (D), promises an example (B), then describes the buffalo’s obedience to the child’s guidance (C), and finally shows the friendship in action while ploughing (A), leading naturally to S2’s continued field description.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences place the “example” promise (B) after giving the example, or place detailed action (A/C) before the narrator’s clarification (D), weakening flow.

Learning points: (1) Authorial comment/clarification often comes early. (2) “I shall soon give an example” must precede the example. (3) General description can precede specific action. (4) Maintain cause → illustration order. (5) Connect S2 with ploughing context introduced just before it.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. Flaw: Number Two is that deterrence is premised on fear.
A. On the contrary, it is the endless, tireless, confrontational work of those who have had the courage to openly denounce them, the marches, the demonstrations, the films, the outrage-that is what has averted, or perhaps only postponed, nuclear war.
B. It is not some inherent, mystical attribute of nuclear bombs that they automatically inspire thoughts of peace.
C. But fear is premised on knowledge.
D. On an understanding of the true extent and scale of the devastation that nuclear war will wreak.
S2. Deterrence will not and cannot work given the levels of ignorance and illiteracy that hang over our two countries like dense, impenetrable veils. [MTS, 18 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
The sequence C→D explains what fear depends on (knowledge and understanding of devastation), then B denies a mystical “peace” effect of bombs, and A contrasts by crediting activism for averting war; this leads logically to S2 about ignorance defeating deterrence.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences break the dependency chain “fear → knowledge → understanding,” or place the contrast (“On the contrary”) without a proper preceding claim.

Learning points: (1) Track connector words: “But,” “On,” “On the contrary.” (2) Keep cause–explanation together (C with D). (3) “On the contrary” needs a prior statement to contrast (fits after B). (4) End should align with S2’s conclusion about ignorance. (5) Build the paragraph around the main idea introduced in S1.

question.en:
**Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.**

S1. As temperatures climbed, the trees proliferated and came into competition with each other.
A. Each banyan spread out farther, sometimes doubling back on itself for safety.
B. Under pressure, it evolved and adapted.
C. Always it grew higher and crept wider, protecting its parent stem as its rivals multiplied, dropping down trunk after trunk, throwing out branch after branch, until at last it learnt the trick of growing into its neighbour banyan, forming a thicket against which no other tree could strive.
D. On this continent, the banyan, thriving in the heat and using its complex system of self-rooting branches, gradually established ascendancy over the other species.
S2. Their complexity became unrivalled, their immortality established. [MTS, 18 Feb 2025, Shift 3]

solution.en:
D sets the banyan as the focus and its ascendancy, B follows with adaptation under pressure, A gives a concrete growth behavior, and C expands this into the detailed process culminating in dominance—then S2 concludes with unmatched complexity.

Why other options are wrong: The wrong sequences either introduce detailed growth mechanics before establishing banyan’s dominance (D) or disrupt the general-to-specific flow.

Learning points: (1) Move from general context (S1) to main subject (D). (2) Cause/pressure → adaptation (B). (3) Short detail (A) can precede longer elaboration (C). (4) Keep the most descriptive/long sentence near the end before the conclusion. (5) Ensure S2 feels like a natural wrap-up.
